name: Chandrayaan-1
one_line: India's first mission to the Moon, an orbiter that found evidence of water molecules on the lunar surface.
key_facts: Launched 22 October 2008 on a PSLV-XL (PSLV-C11) from Sriharikota.
Carried an orbiter plus the Moon Impact Probe, which struck the lunar south pole.
Found widespread evidence of water/hydroxyl molecules on the Moon.
Achieved about 95% of its objectives before contact was lost in August 2009.
org_unit: U R Rao Satellite Centre, Bengaluru

name: Chandrayaan-2
one_line: India's second lunar mission, an orbiter-lander-rover combination whose Vikram lander crashed during its final descent.
key_facts: Launched 22 July 2019 on a GSLV Mk III (GSLV Mk III-M1) from Sriharikota.
Comprised an orbiter, the Vikram lander, and the Pragyan rover.
Contact with Vikram was lost at about 2 km altitude during the 7 September 2019 landing attempt.
The orbiter survived and continues to operate in lunar orbit, returning science data.
status: Orbiter operational; lander/rover lost on landing
org_unit: U R Rao Satellite Centre, Bengaluru

name: Chandrayaan-3
one_line: India's successful soft-landing mission that made India the fourth country to land on the Moon and the first near the lunar south pole.
key_facts: Launched 14 July 2023 on a LVM3 (LVM3-M4) from Sriharikota.
Vikram lander touched down on 23 August 2023, now marked as National Space Day.
Made India the 4th nation to soft-land on the Moon and the first to land near the south pole.
Carried the Pragyan rover, which explored the landing site before both went into sleep mode at lunar night.
org_unit: U R Rao Satellite Centre, Bengaluru

name: Gaganyaan
one_line: ISRO's human spaceflight programme, aiming to send Indian astronauts to low Earth orbit aboard an Indian-built crew module.
key_facts: Uncrewed test flights (Gaganyaan-1 and onward) are targeted before any crewed launch.
The first crewed flight will follow the uncrewed test flights; its launch date has not been finalised.
The programme has already flown a Test Vehicle Abort Mission (TV-D1, October 2023) to validate the crew escape system.
Will also feed into India's planned Bharatiya Antariksh Station (Indian space station).
_notes: Crewed flight has slipped repeatedly; last seen targeted ~2027. Re-check before quoting a date.
status: In development (uncrewed test flights in progress; crewed flight not yet launched)

name: Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission)
one_line: India's first interplanetary mission, which put a spacecraft into Mars orbit on its very first attempt.
key_facts: Launched 5 November 2013 on a PSLV-XL (PSLV-C25) from Sriharikota.
Entered Mars orbit on 24 September 2014, making ISRO the fourth space agency to reach Mars.
India became the first country to succeed at Mars on its first attempt.
Operated far beyond its planned 6-month life; lost contact during an eclipse in April 2022 after propellant exhaustion, with ISRO declaring the mission non-recoverable around October 2022.
status: Mission complete (lost contact April 2022; declared non-recoverable October 2022)
org_unit: U R Rao Satellite Centre, Bengaluru

name: Aditya-L1
one_line: India's first dedicated mission to study the Sun, stationed in a halo orbit around the Sun-Earth L1 point.
key_facts: Launched 2 September 2023 on a PSLV-XL (PSLV-C57) from Sriharikota.
Inserted into its halo orbit around the Sun-Earth L1 point on 6 January 2024.
Carries seven payloads studying the photosphere, chromosphere, and corona plus solar wind.
L1 is about 1.5 million km from Earth; the halo orbit takes about 178 days to complete.
org_unit: U R Rao Satellite Centre, Bengaluru

name: PSLV
one_line: ISRO's four-stage workhorse launch vehicle, used for the large majority of India's satellite and interplanetary launches.
key_facts: First flew as PSLV-D1 on 20 September 1993 (that flight failed); first success was PSLV-D2 on 15 October 1994.
A four-stage rocket alternating solid and liquid propulsion stages.
Launched Chandrayaan-1, Mangalyaan, and Aditya-L1, among many other missions.
Nicknamed ISRO's 'workhorse' for its long, reliable launch record.

name: GSLV Mk-III / LVM3
one_line: ISRO's most powerful operational launch vehicle, now called LVM3, used for heavy satellites and crewed Gaganyaan flights.
key_facts: First orbital test launch on 5 June 2017 from Sriharikota, after a sub-orbital test in December 2014.
Three-stage vehicle combining two solid strap-on boosters, a liquid core, and a cryogenic upper stage.
ISRO's heaviest launcher, able to place about 4,000 kg into geostationary transfer orbit.
Launched Chandrayaan-2, Chandrayaan-3, and is the designated launcher for crewed Gaganyaan flights.
_notes: Dropped the LEO payload figure (10,000 kg was unverified; ISRO has also quoted ~8,000 kg). GTO ~4,000 kg kept.

name: NavIC
one_line: India's own regional satellite navigation system, providing positioning services over India and the surrounding region.
key_facts: Originally built as IRNSS; renamed NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation) in 2016.
Constellation of 7 satellites launched between 2013 and 2016, all via PSLV.
Covers India and a region extending about 1,500 km beyond its borders.
Offers a civilian Standard Positioning Service and a Restricted Service for strategic users.
org_unit: U R Rao Satellite Centre, Bengaluru

name: RISAT
one_line: ISRO's series of radar imaging satellites that can observe Earth day or night and through cloud cover.
key_facts: RISAT-2 launched April 2009 as India's first satellite carrying a synthetic aperture radar (SAR).
RISAT-1, India's first indigenously developed radar imaging satellite, launched April 2012.
Uses synthetic aperture radar for all-weather, day-and-night Earth observation.
Used for disaster management, agriculture, and border surveillance applications.
org_unit: U R Rao Satellite Centre, Bengaluru

name: Vikram lander
one_line: The lunar lander named after Vikram Sarabhai that flew on Chandrayaan-2 and successfully soft-landed on Chandrayaan-3.
key_facts: Named after Vikram Sarabhai, the founder of India's space programme.
Flew twice: crashed during descent on Chandrayaan-2 (2019); soft-landed successfully on Chandrayaan-3 (23 August 2023).
Landed near the Moon's south pole, a first for any country.
Carried the Pragyan rover down to the lunar surface and deployed it via a ramp.
org_unit: U R Rao Satellite Centre, Bengaluru

name: Pragyan rover
one_line: The small six-wheeled rover that explored the lunar surface near the south pole after the Chandrayaan-3 landing.
key_facts: Name means 'wisdom' in Sanskrit; carried inside the Vikram lander.
Deployed onto the lunar surface after the Chandrayaan-3 landing on 23 August 2023.
Carried instruments to study the chemical and elemental composition of the lunar soil.
Designed to operate for one lunar day (about 14 Earth days) before going into sleep mode.
status: Mission complete (operations ended at lunar nightfall, September 2023)
org_unit: U R Rao Satellite Centre, Bengaluru

name: SDSC Sriharikota
one_line: ISRO's primary launch site, on a barrier island on India's east coast, from which nearly all Indian orbital launches take place.
key_facts: First launch from the site was the RH-125 Rohini-series sounding rocket on 9 October 1971.
Renamed Satish Dhawan Space Centre in 2002, after former ISRO chairman Satish Dhawan.
Located on Sriharikota island, Andhra Pradesh, between Pulicat Lake and the Bay of Bengal.
Chosen for its near-equatorial location and large uninhabited safety zone for eastward launches.

name: VSSC Thiruvananthapuram
one_line: ISRO's lead centre for launch vehicle and rocket technology, headquartered in Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala.
key_facts: Traces its origins to the Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station, established in 1962.
Formally consolidated and named after Vikram Sarabhai in 1972, under the new Department of Space.
Thumba was chosen for its proximity to the geomagnetic equator, ideal for upper-atmosphere research.
Lead centre for developing India's launch vehicles, including SLV-3, ASLV, PSLV, and GSLV.

name: ISTRAC Bengaluru
aliases: ISRO Telemetry Tracking and Command Network
one_line: ISRO's ground segment network, responsible for tracking and commanding satellites and launch vehicles from Bengaluru.
key_facts: Established on 6 September 1976.
Headquartered in Bengaluru, with a network of ground stations across India and abroad (including Mauritius, Brunei, and Indonesia).
Provides telemetry, tracking, and command (TTC) support through a satellite's entire mission life.
Also handles orbit determination, attitude control support, and network coordination for ISRO missions.

name: NISAR
one_line: A joint NASA-ISRO Earth observation satellite carrying dual-frequency radar to track changes in Earth's land and ice surfaces.
key_facts: Launched 30 July 2025 on ISRO's GSLV-F16 from Sriharikota.
First satellite to carry both an L-band and an S-band synthetic aperture radar.
Scans nearly all of Earth's land and ice surfaces every 12 days.
Tracks glacier flow, earthquake and volcano dynamics, and ecosystem changes.
org_unit: U R Rao Satellite Centre, Bengaluru (joint mission with NASA/JPL)

name: Aryabhata
one_line: India's first satellite, named after the ancient astronomer, launched with Soviet assistance in 1975.
key_facts: Launched 19 April 1975 on a Soviet Kosmos-3M rocket from Kapustin Yar.
Made India the 11th nation to place a satellite in orbit.
Carried instruments for X-ray astronomy, aeronomy, and solar physics experiments.
A power system failure ended most experiments within days, though the satellite itself orbited for years.
status: Mission complete (decayed from orbit in February 1992)

name: INSAT
one_line: India's long-running series of multipurpose geostationary satellites for telecommunications, broadcasting, and weather monitoring.
key_facts: First satellite, INSAT-1A, launched 10 April 1982 (it was later abandoned in 1983 due to technical failures).
INSAT-1B, launched in 1983, became the first fully operational satellite in the series.
Combines telecommunications, television broadcasting, meteorology, and search-and-rescue payloads on one platform.
One of the largest domestic communication satellite systems in the Asia-Pacific region.
status: Operational (multiple generations of satellites in the series)
org_unit: U R Rao Satellite Centre, Bengaluru

name: Cartosat
one_line: ISRO's series of high-resolution Earth observation satellites used mainly for cartography and mapping.
key_facts: First satellite of the series, Cartosat-1, launched 5 May 2005 on PSLV-C6 from Sriharikota.
Part of India's remote sensing programme, used for large-scale and topographic mapping.
Provides stereoscopic imagery, useful for generating terrain and elevation data.
The series has continued across multiple generations for both civilian and defence applications.
org_unit: U R Rao Satellite Centre, Bengaluru

name: Shukrayaan
one_line: ISRO's planned orbiter mission to Venus, India's first mission to explore an inner planet.
key_facts: Government-approved Venus Orbiter Mission; the launch date has not been finalised.
Planned to launch on an LVM3 rocket carrying a suite of scientific instruments.
Will use aerobraking to lower its orbit around Venus after arrival.
Intended to study Venus's atmosphere, surface, and geological activity.
_notes: Launch last seen targeted ~2028 and has shifted before; instrument count (~19) unconfirmed.
org_unit: U R Rao Satellite Centre, Bengaluru
